title: Week 4 Mastery Quiz — Rivers, Cities, Law, and Government

questions.prompt: Which feature best distinguishes a city-state?
choices: A city and its surrounding territory function as an independent political unit.
All cities are governed by one universal emperor.
Its economy excludes agriculture and trade.
Its laws apply equally to every neighboring society.
questions.explanation: A city-state is an independent political unit centered on a city and its surrounding territory.

questions.prompt: Why did early governments and temples expand writing and accounting systems?
choices: To eliminate oral communication
To record resources, labor, taxes or tribute, and obligations
To make agriculture unnecessary
To prevent all political competition
questions.explanation: Administrative institutions needed durable records for resources, labor, and obligations.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by comparing the Nile and Tigris-Euphrates systems?
choices: River geography dictated identical political systems.
All river floods were equally predictable.
Similar agricultural opportunities could produce different political responses and institutions.
Cities could develop only where deserts surrounded rivers.
questions.explanation: Geographic opportunities and constraints matter, but societies respond through institutions and choices rather than a single predetermined path.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest caution when using a collection associated with Hammurabi to reconstruct everyday life?
choices: Written evidence has no historical value.
Legal cases reveal only agricultural technology.
The collection proves every rule was enforced identically.
It reveals legal ideals and social distinctions but cannot by itself prove everyday enforcement or experience.
questions.explanation: Law collections are valuable evidence of norms and categories, but practice requires corroboration.

questions.prompt: A bureaucracy is best understood as:
choices: an administrative system of officials and offices
a wedge-shaped writing system
goods delivered to a ruler
an independent city and its territory
questions.explanation: Bureaucracy refers to organized administrative offices and officials.

questions.prompt: Why can grain surplus strengthen state capacity?
choices: Surplus guarantees equal wealth.
Stored and collected resources can support specialists, public works, administration, and emergency reserves.
Surplus removes the need for labor coordination.
Surplus proves that rulers were legitimate.
questions.explanation: Surplus can finance activities beyond immediate household consumption, increasing institutional capacity.

questions.prompt: Which observation most directly supports the claim that early legal systems could formalize inequality?
choices: Rivers were used for transportation.
Writing was used for accounting.
Penalties or obligations could differ according to social status or category.
Cities contained specialized labor.
questions.explanation: Different legal treatment by status provides direct evidence of formally recognized social inequality.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes written law from the broader principle of rule of law?
choices: They are identical concepts in every historical society.
Rule of law means rulers never use administrators.
Written law exists only in democracies.
A society may have written rules without consistently subjecting political authority to known, general legal constraints.
questions.explanation: Written rules alone do not establish the stronger institutional principle that authority itself is constrained by law.

questions.prompt: A historian comparing a Mesopotamian law case with an Egyptian labor record is primarily using corroboration to:
choices: compare different evidence to test, refine, or limit a historical interpretation
prove that the two societies were politically identical
replace contextual analysis with a single source
assume administrative records are neutral
questions.explanation: Corroboration compares independent evidence to strengthen, complicate, or limit claims.

questions.prompt: Which explanation best answers why early cities developed more complex systems of authority?
choices: Large populations automatically become monarchies.
Dense populations and concentrated resources created coordination, allocation, conflict, infrastructure, and recordkeeping problems that institutions attempted to manage.
Writing caused rivers to flood predictably.
Every early city developed the same government for the same reason.
questions.explanation: Urban concentration created recurring coordination problems, while institutional responses varied across societies.

shortResponse.prompt: Using at least two specific pieces of evidence from Week 4, explain why early cities developed new systems of law, labor, recordkeeping, and authority. Include one benefit of coordination and one way those systems could reinforce inequality or concentrated power.
shortResponse.exemplar: Full-credit work makes a defensible causal claim, uses at least two accurate Week 4 details, connects evidence to reasoning, and includes a qualification about inequality, enforcement, or variation among societies.
